newsitem.title: GUAM: KAL survivors in good mental shape but grieve dead.
newsitem.headline: KAL survivors in good mental shape but grieve dead.

text.p: Survivors of the fiery crash of Korean Air Lines (KAL) Flight 801 on Guam have shown great mental strength amid the anguish felt for their dead loved ones, a Korean doctor said on Friday.
"All of those we've treated are incredibly strong mentally, especially considering their experience and their loss," said Dr Moon G. Yoon of Guam Memorial Hospital.
"So far no psychological help has been needed -- none," said the Korean-born doctor, head of the operating room at the hospital, where 12 of the 27 crash survivors are being treated.
The patients, most of whom were being readied to fly home to South Korean hospitals later on Friday, "almost to an individual asked about loved ones on the flight as soon as they awoke."
Psychiatrists and counsellors were on call around the clock, said Tyrone Taitano, the hospital administrator.
Survivor Lee Chang-woo, a 28-year-old Seoul businessman, told Reuters in a bedside interview the physical pain from a broken ankle and several serious cuts had mostly passed.
But asked if he felt lucky to survive while more than 200 perished on a jungle hillside nearly 48 hours earlier, Lee spoke only of his fiancee and three friends who didn't live.
"I don't know what to think about my being spared, because my friends and my girlfriend are all dead," said Lee, an employee of the South Korean conglomerate LG Group.
Lee, who spoke in a weak voice, said he thought the jumbo jet was about to land.
"Then there was violent shaking and I blacked out. When I came to, it was pitch black, I had lost my eyeglasses and I smelled fuel all around me.
"I called out my fiancee's name, but got no answer. That's when I got out of the plane and limped away," he said.
Lee said the only thing he wanted to do upon return to South Korea "is take a good long rest".
"Then I want to go back to work and work hard."
Staff at Guam Memorial Hospital had been unable to tell survivors of the precise fate of fellow passengers, because investigators had not published a list of the dead, Taitano said.
"We had to say their status was 'missing'," he said, adding that most survivors appeared to assume the worst.
